I am genuinely amazed by this story. I really enjoy its power system, and I honestly think it's one of the best I've encountered, if not the best, then at least in the top three of all the novels I've read. The MC is also really well-written.

First of all, the world-building.

I love it when a story has countless unexplored places and mysteries waiting to be uncovered. This novel does an excellent job of creating a world so vast that it's almost impossible to comprehend its true scale. There is always something new to discover, and the sheer size of the universe makes it feel like we've barely scratched the surface.

The power system is also peak.

I hate power systems where everything depends on natural talent and there's little to nothing you can do to overcome your limitations. Here, however, almost anything feels possible. Yes, bloodlines matter a lot, but if you look at the story of a certain snake, it's stated that he started with practically nothing and still managed to reach the very peak. He was already incredibly powerful even as a C-grade.

I really appreciate how the power system allows for so many different paths to strength rather than making everything dependent on what someone was born with.

Now, onto the MC.

Jake isn't exactly the type of protagonist I usually prefer, or at least he wasnt at the start, but he adapted and developed surprisingly quickly. He learned to accept a lot of things, and his character improved significantly because of it. I especially enjoy the struggles he faces and the challenges he has to overcome. 

Another thing I really appreciate is the skills and their descriptions.

Almost every upgrade eventually gets used and remains relevant in upcoming fights. The fights themselves are really well-structured and follow the established logic of the power system. The power scaling is also handled really well and doesn't become overly chaotic or inconsistent.

One potential downside for some readers is the sheer amount of text, especially since certain abilities have incredibly long descriptions. Personally, though, I actually enjoy reading them. Those details often become relevant during fights and help explain how events unfold. Because of this, Jake's actions rarely feel like random abilities or solutions that suddenly appear out of nowhere without being established beforehand. I can understand why some people might want to skip those descriptions, but I personally find them worthwhile.

Overall, this novel is definitely in my top three favorites, right alongside LOTM and RI.

Absolute peak. If LOTM and RI are a 10/10 for me, then The Primal Hunter is easily a 9.5/10.

I would definitely recommend giving it a read.

A mixed bag for me.

Pros.  The LitRPG elements (skills, levels, etc.) are quite good, and the overall progression is great, if a little slower in the later parts.

The fights are the highlights of this novel and are the main reason I stuck around for as long as I did. Some fights that go on for quite a few chapters are among the best I've read in recent times.

The world-building, especially the records, was interesting even if somewhat unoriginal.

Some of the side characters, especially Sylphie ,Sandy and the glorious minaga, are good, and the author does try to give many of them time to flesh out their characters. I also quite enjoyed the dynamic between Jake and Villy.

Cons:-Jake is one of the most uninteresting, hypocritical, and boring MCs I've come across. As one comment put it, he's like a 15yearold in the body of a 27yearold. This is especially bad early on,where he's also edgy.It improves later, and the author tries to give him some character development,though he fails massively.He's also incredibly inconsistent.I wish the author had just made him a generic powerfantasy MC, which would at least be tolerable.Most of his power is handed to him, which isn't an issue by itself.It's the way he carries himself with that power that irks me.My biggest issue is his morality.

He has no problem massacring entire tribes of innocent sentient creatures for levels.He's also best friends with an evil snake god who has genocided cities,planets,and even half a universe, and all he does is call it a "d*ck move."Yet when someone else does something far less extreme,he starts clutching his pearls.

The dragon arc is a perfect example.he needs to kill someone for progression, so instead of accepting that he's a hunter who kills for power,the story bends over backwards to find a "bad" dragon so he can kill her while still being the good guy. The constant justification is annoying when he's already done arguably worse himself.The slavery aspect is another shitshow. Jake hates slavery, yet his best friend runs an Order where slavery is openly practiced and he never tries to adress it or fight back. Jake can genocide innocent tribes for EXP but draws the line at slavery. The author tries so hard to give him a moral bottom line that it only makes him look hypocritical.If he were simply ruthless, that would be fine.I just wish the author would stop trying to paint him as a decent person.

-The dialogue can be a major turnoff.The grammar is fine,but the banter feels forced and stilted,like someone's idea of good banter rather than natural conversation.

-MC is never in any real danger of losing.The stakes are as low as they can be.

-Nevermore.

Overall: 6/10.Read it if you're looking for something to turn your brain off and watch the numbers go up. If you can tolerate one of the worst MCs out there, there's still plenty to enjoy: the fights are awesome, the world-building is good enough, and the progression is pretty satisfying if a little slow.For what it's worth, I managed to read all 1,300 chapters while actively hating the MC. It's the good kind of slop.

The Primal Hunter world is quite interesting, and the author has written it well, but I hate the MC. Everything is handed to him, from his bloodline to somehow meeting Viper and becoming his true Blessed. Honestly, any Primordial would have made a better MC.

And then there's the cringe. When he pummeled those two girls for bullying his favorite maid-slave girl, I felt the second-hand embarrassment in my bones.

The story isn't tagged as a harem, which is one of the reasons I started reading it. But after making the Valhalla girl his friend with benefits, he starts thinking about relationships with the demoness goat girl and even his maid-slave girl. I also don't understand why he's preaching about the morality of slavery and trying to justify himself to a guy who literally eats planets for breakfast.

Did I forget about Mrs. Prodigy, whose only purpose seems to be letting the MC farm aura in Viper's sect? Am I missing anyone?

So I decided to drop the novel there. The Nevermore arc already looked boring as hell anyway. Up to that point, the story was only tolerable. I don't mind possible love interests if there's ultimately just one "wifey" by the end of the series. But it feels like he'll just keep sleeping with every new woman he meets before moving on to the next.

I wouldn't have spent so much time hating on this novel if it hadn't wasted so much of my time before hinting at becoming a harem. If it had been upfront about that from the beginning, I simply wouldn't have bothered reading it. It's not like the story was particularly enjoyable up to that point either—it was high-tier slop at best, carried only by a few interesting and unique characters.

My perseverance in pushing through, hoping it would eventually get better, was on the same level as Fang Yuan's. But in the end, all I was left with was despair, hopelessness, and regret.

To open with this: While it's a non-factor early on, if you love concepts/laws from cultivation stories, read this. You WILL love it if you get close to the current chapters. I read this on a whim as I was curious about its popularity. What I didn't expect to get was a litRPG that isn't shy to let the progression speak for itself. The world-building is sublime as the system complements the power system. It is thorough with the implications of the power in the multiverse as it tends to answer a lot of questions throughout the story. The gods' personalities are done fantastically, granted a part of it is the MC factor. I do think there are some flaws, however. While the first arc (the Tutorial) can be done better, and the chapters introducing the side characters (they are important to enjoy them. do not skip.) could've been embedded better to the story, sometimes the author, once every 300 something chapters, give and take, decides to write a milder mini-arc to justify the leveling up.

I give it this rating for several reasons.

It’s a good, decent story to read. The characters are quite good, and the first part of the tutorial is honestly the “worst” part; as the story progresses, the plot gets better. However, from a certain point on, I feel that the bloodline becomes too powerful to solve the situations the protagonist faces.

Now, this doesn’t mean I didn’t enjoy the novel a lot. I’m up to date with the Patreon, and I honestly like it quite a bit. That said, if you’re looking for a novel that shows more hardship for the protagonist, this wouldn’t be the one.

Primal Hunter has good system-building, with Primordials, System Events, Gods, Evolutions, and many other elements. The story is interesting, and the supporting characters are good.

Highly recommended if you’re looking for a progression story with level development, but objectively, it deserves this rating because of how the plot is developed.
